posts.caption:
The numbers are becoming something we can design around.

After generating and studying synthetic cylinder-port geometries, Wahoo Intelligence has created its first editable, parametric 3D cylinder CAD foundation. Independent geometric checks confirmed the source-to-CAD mapping.

Changing the provisional occupied-space outer envelope from 94 to 96 mm regenerated the model while preserving the bore and accepted port contours. That is parameter propagation, rather than a complete redraw.

The digital study also preserved a 0.6 mm conflict between a provisional head envelope and the corrected piston crown: a question to resolve before release, not a defect in manufactured hardware.

This is preliminary CAD. The analytic shell remains unjoined; it is not a manufacturing-ready solid, and no cylinder hardware has been manufactured or physically validated by this milestone.

Next comes the complete engine architecture: internal components, cooling, standard purchased hardware, custom CNC-machined parts, a living BOM and integration with the hull and jet pump.

Follow the build as Wahoo moves from digital research toward physical engineering.
posts.title: From simulation to 3D design.

cards.alt: From simulation to 3D design. Large blue-grey source-derived cylinder geometry on graphite, showing the accepted exhaust aperture and two transfer apertures. Preliminary CAD, with an unjoined analytic shell; not manufactured hardware.

Digital geometry. Engineering precision. Actual saved curved bore aperture loops on a pale field: one exhaust opening and two transfer openings. Source-to-CAD correspondence checks passed. These raster presentation views are not manufacturing drawings.

One parameter. A new configuration. Two actual saved CAD-derived cylinder projections compare provisional 94 mm and 96 mm occupied-space outer envelopes. Outer radius increases by approximately 1 mm while bore and accepted port contours remain unchanged. No hardware dimension release.

Every millimeter matters. Actual corrected piston and aperture context appears beside a clearly magnified, not-to-scale schematic of the 0.6 mm provisional head-envelope overlap with the corrected piston crown. A dimensional conflict to resolve before release; no manufactured hardware defect is established.

Next: the complete engine. Actual cylinder geometry is central to a clearly labeled conceptual development roadmap, linked to cylinder head, cooling, fuel injection, exhaust, crankcase, crankshaft, bearings and seals, and jet-pump fit. Surrounding systems are planned, not complete verified CAD. Follow the build.

posts.title: The shortlist comes alive
posts.caption:
A shortlist becomes more useful when we see how it behaves.

With Wahoo Intelligence, 41 generated port designs became eight dynamic histories: five accepted records reused and three new studies. Similar screening totals can lead to different pressure histories. Changing the transfer ports can also change exhaust transport, even with the same exhaust geometry.

This is one unheated synthetic revolution at 3000 RPM over 20 ms, not a power prediction or physical engine validation. The next design questions must account for combined effects, ring support, cooling, manufacturing and fit.

Follow the build as Wahoo’s engine development continues.

cards.alt: Dark Wahoo card titled The shortlist comes alive. Eight outlined oval study identities read 001, 011, 007, 013, 009, 003, 004 and 020. A prominent 8 investigated is paired with 41 generated. Five dynamic histories were reused and three are new. These marks identify synthetic cases and do not depict components.

Pale card titled Eight ways to ask why. Eight deliberately nonproportional aperture schematics: 001 reference; 011 wider exhaust; 007 exhaust timing and height; 013 transfer width; 009 transfer timing and area; 003 tapered exhaust; 004 split exhaust; 020 staged transfer. These are qualitative symbols, not actual CAD contours or dimensions.

Dark plot titled Similar screen totals. Different histories. Cases 007 and 011 have prescribed-pressure exhaust screening capacities about 0.47 percent apart. Their actual selected pressure nodes are joined without smoothing. Horizontal axis crank angle 0 to 360 degrees; vertical absolute cylinder pressure 0 to 1600 kPa. Both fall from 100 kPa, recover during gas exchange and rise during final compression; 007 ends near 1385 kPa and 011 near 1449 kPa. Synthetic 3000 RPM, 20 ms, no heat input.

Pale card titled Same exhaust. A different response. A conceptual transfer–cylinder–exhaust connection diagram has no flow arrows. Comparing 009 with 013, changed transfer design with unchanged exhaust geometry gives 6.193 percent greater transfer inward mass and 5.613 percent greater net exhaust outward mass. Timing and area change together in this synthetic single revolution.

Dark card titled Generate ideas. Test the system. A new conceptual method diagram connects timing, width and shape to candidate marks and combined effects, then to physical constraints: ring support, cooling, manufacturing and fit. A better question comes before a production decision. The graphic describes a source-based method; physical validation remains open.

posts.title: 41 designs. Eight better questions.
posts.caption:
41 port designs. Eight better questions.

Wahoo Intelligence generated 41 distinct synthetic cylinder-port configurations, then screened all 41 under the same prescribed pressures. The results show how port families, widths and opening times change flow capacity, helping us choose what to investigate next.

A useful contrast: A23-007 and A23-011 show similar outward exhaust totals—534.665 and 537.180 mg—yet first open at 86° and 90°. Similar totals can hide different timing.

Eight designs are shortlisted for the next comparison: five have qualified historical dynamic records to reuse; three await dynamic simulation, proposed for A26. This is a development shortlist, not a ranking of the best engines.

The screen does not predict power, torque, trapped charge, scavenging or rider performance. Mechanical assessment and physical validation are still ahead.

Follow the build.

cards.alt: Dark Wahoo cover with a monumental white 41 and text: The search gets wider. 41 port designs. One controlled screen. Forty-one small outlined rectangles form a repeated pattern. They are explicitly schematic marks, not a geometry atlas. Synthetic design study.

Pale card titled Four ways to open. Four newly drawn nonproportional schematics show rectangular, tapered, split and staged port families in blue. Labels explain a common starting point; width changes with height; separate openings; openings begin at different times. These are qualitative schematics, not actual contours or dimensions.

Dark card titled 41 designs. 41 screening results. Scatter plot of all 41 accepted source records: exhaust gross outward capacity in milligrams on the horizontal axis, transfer gross inward capacity in milligrams vertically. Eight shortlisted records are white; the others blue. Some points overlap without jitter. The graph shows prescribed-pressure gross boundary totals, not engine performance.

Pale card titled Similar totals. Different timing. Two bars share a zero-based scale from 0 to 600 mg. A23-007 has 534.665 mg exhaust outward capacity; A23-011 has 537.180 mg. A separate linear angle strip from 80 to 100 degrees marks first exhaust opening at 86 degrees for 007 and 90 degrees for 011. These are prescribed-pressure screen results, not predicted engine output.

Dark closing card shows 8 designs shortlisted from 41 screened. Eight schematic blocks carry candidate suffixes001,003,004,011,013,007,009,020. Five filled blocks identify qualified historical dynamic records to reuse; three hollow blocks identify pending dynamic cases proposed for A26. Text: Next: dynamic simulation. Follow the build. A useful shortlist, not a performance ranking.

posts.title: The cylinder responds.
posts.caption:
Same exhaust geometry. Different exhaust flow.

That is the interesting connection in Wahoo’s latest simulator milestone. We compared five generated cylinder-port designs with a model that updates cylinder mass and energy, derives pressure and temperature, and feeds the changing state into the next gas-flow calculation.

For G001-01 and G001-05, the exhaust geometry is identical. Changing the transfer-port geometry changes the cylinder response—and the exhaust stream. More flow does not establish a better design.

This is a numerically qualified synthetic study: one initial-value revolution at 3,000 rpm, with zero combustion heat. It is not a physically tested engine or a performance result.

Follow the build as we connect the next pieces.

cards.alt: Dark Wahoo card titled “The cylinder responds.” Accepted synthetic G001-01 and G001-05 pressure–volume trajectories are drawn in blue solid and pale dashed lines. Axes show absolute pressure from 0 to 1.8 MPa and cylinder volume from 0 to 140 cubic centimetres. The paths are open initial-value trajectories, not a repeating cycle. Text: Geometry changes the state. The state changes the flow. One synthetic revolution, 3,000 rpm, zero combustion heat.

Pale card titled “One cylinder. A feedback loop.” A fresh qualitative control-volume schematic shows transfer and exhaust calculation links beside a cylinder-state block marked mass plus energy, pressure and temperature. A lower connector runs from the updated state back to the next flow calculation. The graphic is schematic, not exact G001 geometry; arrows show calculation links. Original shaded Wahoo symbol at upper right.

Dark card titled “Same start. Different response.” All five accepted synthetic G001 cylinder absolute-pressure histories share common axes of 0–360 crank-angle degrees and 0–3.2 MPa. Blue and pale solid, dashed and dotted traces identify G001-01 through G001-05. The histories remain separate at the final compression endpoint. Text identifies an initial-value study, not a repeating firing cycle.

Pale card titled “Same exhaust. Different flow.” G001-01 and G001-05 share identical exhaust geometry and differ in transfer geometry. On a common zero-based linear bar scale, transfer inflow is 229.102 versus 136.027 mg; accumulated outward exhaust transfer is 204.256 versus 128.826 mg. Text states that outward totals exclude backflow, which also occurs, and gives no performance ranking. The study is synthetic.

Dark blue milestone card titled “From shape to a system.” Dated 26 October 2026. Three steps read: five port geometries generated; synthetic gas exchange modeled; dynamic cylinder numerically qualified. Text: Physical validation is still ahead. Follow the build. An original shaded Wahoo symbol anchors the upper left.

posts.title: Same test. Different flow.
posts.caption:
A port is more than the moment it opens. We put five synthetic layouts through the same controlled comparison to see how the opening shape carries through to flow.

The reference and taper share the same 90°/270° exhaust events, yet the taper transfers about 41.6% less exhaust mass in this model. That is a difference to understand, not a performance benefit or a winner.

This is a saved synthetic study at 3,000 rpm: one 20 ms revolution, with an imposed pressure change at 180°. Cylinder feedback and physical engine validation are still ahead. The bars show separate boundary-stream totals, not trapped charge or horsepower.

Which part would you like us to unpack next: port shape, pressure or cylinder feedback?

cards.alt: Graphite cover reading Same test. Different flow. Five genuine source developed-wall layouts appear in separate rows: G001-01 reference, G001-02 earlier exhaust, G001-03 tapered exhaust, G001-04 split exhaust and G001-05 staged transfers. Exhaust polygons are orange; transfer polygons are cyan. The cylindrical seam is at each end. These are synthetic layouts, not accepted candidate CAD or a physical cylinder test.

White card reading The shape of an opening. Reference versus taper: same 90°/270° events. Full saved exhaust developed-area curves are plotted in square millimetres against crank angle from 0 to 360 degrees. The five candidate colours and source series order are retained; reference 01 and staged-transfer 05 overlap. Developed wall area is not calibrated effective flow area.

Graphite card reading Watch the pressure step. Full saved exhaust mass-flow curves show positive outflow in grams per second against crank angle. At 180 degrees the cylinder proxy pressure is imposed from 160 to 100 kPa, producing the discontinuity. All source samples, including left and right limits, are retained. Reference 01 and 05 overlap. Synthetic 3,000 rpm, 20 ms study without cylinder feedback.

White card reading Total flow. More questions. Paired bars from accepted saved values retain five candidate colours. Each pair is left exhaust, right transfer, with forward boundary mass in milligrams over one revolution. These are independent stream totals, not trapped charge or horsepower.

Blue graphite typography card with original shaded W mark asks Which question comes next? Port shape. Pressure. Cylinder feedback. A model gives us something to inspect. The next step is something to question. Stay curious. Follow Wahoo's development. Synthetic study; physical validation is still ahead.

posts.title: Meet Leo
posts.caption: Meet Leo, the fictional face of Wahoo’s coordinating AI role. He helps connect questions, specialist work and the evidence behind it. Max owns the decisions, and physical tests still have the final word. A little imagination on the shoreline; a lot of real work behind the build. Follow along.

cards.alt: Cinematic generated scene of Leo, Wahoo’s fictional black and blue AI character, standing alone on a beach and looking toward the sunset horizon beneath dramatic clouds. Subtle digital particles surround one hand. Original Wahoo wordmark and headline “Meet Leo.” Label states fictional AI character, generated scene.

posts.title: Know your machine
posts.caption: The more you understand a machine, the better the questions you can ask about it. We want understanding and care to be part of the ownership experience—from what a control does to how the system can be maintained. That is a design ambition we are still working toward. What would you want explained first?

cards.alt: White editorial card reading “Know your machine” and “Curiosity is part of ownership.” Authentic transparent throttle source linework stands beside “Ask how it works. Ask how to care for it. That’s the ambition.” Original shaded W symbol. Linework is a design concept, not final hardware.

posts.title: When does it open?
posts.caption: Start with a question you can inspect. These are two separate saved synthetic checks: an idealized opening trace, and a pressure response inside a fixed volume. They do not form a connected engine sequence. The opening is not an effective flow area, and the imposed reservoir change is not a real valve or firing event. Both are development fixtures, not measured Wahoo engine performance. Follow the build as better questions become clearer checks.

cards.alt: Blue card asking “When does it open?” Original saved synthetic plot shows idealized opening per unit developed width in millimetres against crank angle after local top dead centre. Solid cyan A and dashed blue B retain all 73 source samples per curve at five-degree intervals without smoothing. Idealized uncapped geometry, not effective flow area. Card 1 of 3.

Graphite card asking “What changes inside?” Original saved synthetic fixed-volume controlled reservoir transition shows absolute cylinder pressure in Pa against fixture time in seconds, with 81 saved states and reservoir change at 0.010 seconds. Imposed boundary change is not a real valve or firing event; not measured engine performance. Card 2 of 3.

White typography card reading “Better questions. Better checks.” Build understanding before making predictions. Software checks are one step; physical validation is still ahead. Original shaded W symbol. Development tool, not measured engine performance. Card 3 of 3.

posts.title: What makes a great ride?
posts.caption: Everyone brings a different idea of a great day on the water. Feeling in control, exploring a new stretch of coastline, or simply finding your own rhythm—what matters most to you? Tell us one thing you would want from your ideal ride. Concept imagery; the Wahoo build is still in development.

cards.alt: Graphite card asking “What makes a great ride?” A previously unused approved fictional concept image shows a helmeted rider and dark board from overhead, surrounded by white wake on dark water. Original landscape image shown proportionally. Label: Concept scene. Invitation: Tell us what matters to you. This is not a physical Wahoo test.

posts.title: Follow the build
posts.caption: Some days the build moves through a new idea. Other days it moves through a better question. We are sharing both: the design, the learning and the work still ahead. Follow Wahoo and come closer to the process.

cards.alt: Cool blue typographic card with the original shaded W symbol and large headline “Follow the build.” Text: The ideas. The questions. The work in between. Invitation: Come closer to Wahoo.

posts.title: Trust the shape behind the numbers
posts.caption: Before we learn from a hull analysis, we check the shape it uses. Our native SubD stays the design master; a separate derived Brep supports analytical sectioning. The recorded surface-sample comparison reached a maximum distance of approximately 0.594 micrometres. That is a discrete position check, not proof of exact agreement everywhere or a manufacturing certificate. Good development starts by knowing what the evidence can tell us.

cards.alt: White card reading “Trust the shape behind the numbers,” with an authentic native bottom-hull zebra inspection rotated so bow is to the right. The stripes are a geometry inspection aid, not flow. Existing background-removed presentation derivative, not new geometry or analysis.

Pale card reading “Compare at the surface.” Transparent source-data top-projection distance map retains R01 X forward and Y port axes in centimetres, and a micrometre distance colour scale. Samples may overlap.

Blue card with 0.594 μm, maximum sampled distance. Native SubD remains master; the derived Brep supports analysis. Explicitly states this is a sampled comparison, not a continuous or manufacturing certificate.

posts.title: Bring the stinger inside
posts.caption: Can an exhaust outlet occupy less space outside its chamber? The internal-stinger concept overlaps the tube with the chamber: the provisional sketch records 195 mm inside and 20 mm outside, 215 mm total, with an 18 mm internal diameter. The current direction is completely straight, with no bends inside the hull. Engine alignment, the tube/baffle junction, cooling, tuning and installed clearances still need work. This is a packaging idea to develop, not a demonstrated power or fit result.

cards.alt: Dark card reading “Bring the stinger inside.” Original section-only sketch shows the internal tube overlapping the chamber. Labels retain provisional dimensions; the historical bend plan is excluded.
White typography card with 195 mm inside the chamber and 20 mm projecting outside; 215 mm total and 18 mm internal diameter. Dimensions are provisional and do not establish tuning or fit.

Blue card reading “Keep it straight. No bends or turns inside the hull.” Lists engine alignment, tube/baffle junction, cooling and service clearances as unresolved; power, tuning and fit are unproven.

posts.title: A clearer route aft
posts.caption: Packaging an engine means making room for the whole system—and for the hands and tools that will service it. The selected Rev03 direction sends the exhaust aft from the cylinder side, replacing the earlier forward loop. Compactness and access are goals; the rough component envelopes do not prove installed fit. The water-jacket cutaway is the provisional Rev01 external-stinger comparison: separate exhaust gas and cooling water, then verify cooling, tuning, clearances and water protection. Each view answers a different design question.

cards.alt: Graphite card reading “A clearer route aft.” Cropped original transparent Rev03 isometric shows provisional engine and exhaust envelopes. Cylinder-side route is selected; fit and tuning remain pending.

White comparison card reading “Make space. Keep access.” Original source views show Rev01 earlier forward loop and Rev03 selected direct-aft route in top views, bow up. These are provisional envelopes; compactness and service access remain goals.

Blue card reading “Gas inside. Water around.” Authentic transparent cutaway shows silver pipe, blue jacket wall and intervening water space. It is the provisional Rev01 unwrapped external-stinger comparison, not the selected installed system.

posts.title: You own it.
posts.caption:
You own it. That’s the idea shaping Wahoo.

We’re developing a jetboard with serviceability and long-term ownership in mind. Understand it. Maintain it. Make it yours.

These are design ambitions as we develop the board.

cards.alt: Original shaded white Wahoo W symbol beside large stacked words YOU OWN IT with a blue period on graphite. Small text: The Wahoo idea. Card 1 of 5.

Ten defined AI roles help investigate Wahoo’s development. Leo connects the work, specialists explore questions, and Isaac challenges consequential conclusions. Max decides what moves forward.

posts.caption:
Riders. Builders. Curious minds.

We want Wahoo to grow with a community that shares what it learns, on the water and in the workshop.

What would you want to understand first?

Concept scene, illustrating an ambition.

posts.title: Inside the simulator.
posts.caption:
Start with movement. Then ask what happens to pressure, heat and waves.

Wahoo’s simulator grows through small, checkable models. These saved schematics and synthetic benchmarks help us test the software before making engine predictions.

They are development tools, not measured engine performance.

cards.alt: Pale poster titled Start with movement. Exact existing 2D piston, rod and crank schematic at its saved 90-degree pose stands to the right of the supporting text: One step toward a model we can question. Label: Saved 2D schematic, not to scale. Card 1 of 5.

Graphite poster titled Less volume. More pressure. Original saved pressure versus volume compression curve, with original axes, units and labels. Compression runs right to left. Synthetic closed-mass adiabatic ideal-gas qualification fixture with no heat input; not a measured Wahoo trace. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster titled Add heat. Check the change. Original synthetic temperature versus time curves show prescribed heating and cooling at fixed mass and volume. Original units and legends retained. No wall-cooling correlation solved. Card 3 of 5.

Graphite poster with a large saved pressure-history plot above the headline Follow the pulse. Exact original axes, sample curves, units and receiver legends are preserved for a stationary uniform linear-acoustic rigid-boundary benchmark. Text: A saved benchmark. One bounded physics question. Not nonlinear exhaust blowdown. Card 4 of 5.

Graphite poster with original Wahoo wordmark, titled What does the model keep? Existing acoustic energy benchmark plot retains units, samples and labels. Text: Energy is part of the check. Engine performance still needs validation. Solid curve: rigid termination retains pulse energy. Dashed curve: absorbing termination lets energy leave. Not a dyno result. Card 5 of 5.

posts.title: Hull development: look closer.
posts.caption:
Look closer.

Hull development means more than choosing a silhouette. We inspect surfaces, cut sections, follow profiles and mark questions for review. Then limited CFD cases explore the interaction with water.

These are geometry studies and early simulation evidence. They do not establish handling, stability or final performance; physical validation is still ahead.

cards.alt: Dark poster titled Look closer. Large crop of the existing native H0 R02 tail surface zebra inspection, with original Wahoo wordmark. Text: The shape behind the ride. Label: H0 R02, surface review, not water flow. Card 1 of 5.

Dark poster titled Slice through the question. Original overlaid transverse tail sections from the derived Brep preserve equal Y and Z scales, original units and station legend. The unchanged legend is enlarged separately below the plot so it no longer covers the curves. Text: The tail changes in three dimensions. Sections help us see how. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster titled Follow the shape. Existing source-derived Brep tail cutaway illustration shows transverse and longitudinal section curves and original C1/C4 witness labels. This is a clipped analytical view; the actual hull remains closed. Text: Sections and profiles. One three-dimensional question. Card 3 of 5.

Pale poster with original black Wahoo symbol. Text: Check the whole surface. A full underside board zebra-pattern image sits directly on the pale background with transparent surroundings. Text: Zebra patterns help us inspect surface continuity. Label: Native surface review, not water flow. Background-removed presentation derivative of the existing native review image, not new geometry or analysis. Card 4 of 5.

Dark poster titled Then ask the water. Actual saved historical CFD20 free-surface field at simulation time 1.579983709 seconds. Conditions printed on artwork: historical 20 km/h, bare board, no rider, closed intake, no jet thrust. Text: Early CFD explores a limited case. Physical testing is still ahead. Not performance validation. Card 5 of 5.

posts.title: Control. In your hand.
posts.caption:
Control in your hand. The design is still open.

We’re exploring how grip, throttle, starting and essential information could come together in one handheld controller. The blue-accent presentation concept introduces the idea; three other visual directions keep the housing and grip discussion open.

The intended features include a progressive trigger, thumb-operated rear starter, top display, left- or right-side lanyard positions, and separate grab-line and cable interfaces. Ergonomics, operation and safety functions still need testing. No final design has been selected.

Which visual direction would you explore—and what would matter most in your hand?

cards.alt: Pale Wahoo poster with original black shaded W symbol. Large words: Control. In your hand. The unchanged blue-accent tc04 handheld-controller concept sits to the right. Text: One interface. Four visual directions. The design stays open. Label: Presentation concept, no final design selected. Card 1 of 5.

Graphite poster headed Keep the grip. Reach the controls. The unchanged tc04 controller concept sits beside five intended functions: progressive trigger for throttle modulation; rear starter for thumb-operated starting; top display for essential operating information; left/right lanyard for stance-aware attachment positions; lower interfaces for grab line and control cable. Label: Design intent, ergonomics and function untested. Card 2 of 5.

Pale poster showing the unchanged tc01 controller concept with open head, visible fasteners and textured grip. Headline: Open expression. Option 01. Original black shaded Wahoo symbol. Label: Visual direction, no final selection. Card 3 of 5.

Blue graphite poster showing the unchanged tc02 controller concept at large scale on the left. Headline: Fuller form. Option 02. Text: A fuller housing. Diagonal grip texture. Blue detailing. Original white Wahoo symbol. Label: Visual direction, no final selection. Card 4 of 5.

Pale poster showing the unchanged tc03 controller concept on the right. Headline: Smoother surfaces. Option 03. Text: A quieter housing treatment. A different grip texture. Question: Which direction would you explore? Original black Wahoo wordmark. Label: Concepts, ergonomics still to be tested. Card 5 of 5.

The feeling we’re working toward.

Last light, open water and a little more time outside. This concept visual imagines the experience behind Wahoo’s development; it is not a photograph of a Wahoo test or a claim of a finished product.

posts.title: Product / design story

cards.alt: A pale blue CAD-derived H0 R03 hull is rotated into a dramatic upright composition on a dark background. “A shape worth a closer look.” The complete hull remains visible. The original shaded white Wahoo W symbol sits at the lower left.
A large cropped detail of the native hull underside crosses a blue-grey background diagonally. “Follow the surface.” The crop is a detail of the approved render, not new geometry.
The native hull side profile sits above a large blue “Shape. Check. Refine.” headline. “Development in progress” qualifies the product stage.

posts.caption:
A shape is where the questions begin.

A perspective, a closer look underneath, then the side profile: three native CAD-derived views of the H0 R03 hull reference. Looking from different angles helps us question the design before making claims about how it will ride.

These are development views, not a finished production board or proof of handling. Which angle would you like to explore?

posts.title: Engineering made simple

cards.alt: “Motion before power.” Native partial-piston linework with schematic crank and rod appears on an open pale background. “Start with something we can check.” The original shaded black Wahoo W symbol sits at the lower right.

“A turn becomes a stroke.” The published simulator’s stronger two-dimensional cylinder, piston, crank and rod schematic is shown at its exact saved 90-degree pose. Schematic components and saved landmarks; not to scale, with no new model run.

“Back. And forth.” A blue curve shows all 361 exact saved nominal piston-pin positions in metres against crank angle from zero to 360 degrees. This is a software motion trace, not an engine performance plot.
“361 positions. One careful check.” A larger cropped native partial-piston linework detail sits above 361 dots. “Software correspondence. Physical validation ahead.”

“Confidence starts with the basics.” An unchanged native hull perspective connects the motion story back to the board being developed. “A development story. One verified step at a time.” The original shaded black Wahoo W symbol sits at the upper right.

posts.caption:
Does it move the way we expect?

The crank turns; the piston moves back and forth. Our nominal software/CAD check compared 361 saved positions. Checking that digital motion is one small step toward a product we can trust.

The linework shows partial source geometry with a schematic mechanism. It does not validate a complete engine, combustion, power, physical reliability or safety. Physical validation remains ahead.

What part of Wahoo would you like us to explain next?
